On today's stock market crash:

As an investor, on days like today, you have to ask yourself one question: What fundamentally changed over the last 24 hours?

The shift in the fundamental backdrop cannot be attributed solely to the Midterm Election results; markets had already largely priced in the outcome.

So, what changed between yesterday and today? What is the fundamental reason for today's decline?

One of the most likely catalysts is growing concern about a potential "ban" on AI, or at the very least, severe regulation of the industry.

Over the last 24 hours, Democratic lawmakers have publicly called for restrictions on advanced AI development, including an outright "ban on artificial superintelligence."

Frankly, an outright ban will not happen.

Such a ban, if even possible to enforce, would effectively mean the US surrendering its position in the global AI race to China.

Does this mean AI is "over" or today's stock market crash marks "the end?" Absolutely not.

Rather, we believe we are witnessing a sudden shift in sentiment colliding with excessive levels of leverage, potentially triggering forced liquidations by several major institutional investors.

Therefore, today's downturn is more technical than fundamental. This is not to discount the concerns around regulation, they are legitimate. But price action right now does not look orderly or rational.

We are in the midst of the biggest technological revolution in human history.

Zoom out and remain calm.

Distribution of Type 1 breakouts is cyclical. It is tied to the momentum cycle of the markets. A period of chop is usually followed by directional moves. 

The strength of the directional moves impact the success of chart patterns in different duration.

Lately short-term chart pattern in duration 2-4 months have been more successful than the >6 months patterns.

Speaking of the dot com bust… We all know the caveat that price analogs are silly and for entertainment purposes only. Yet, the analog between the AI melt-up since April 2025 and the dot com bubble from October 1998 until March 2000 keeps rhyming with uncanny precision. It’s bound to break at some point, but for now both the time dimension and the price magnitude have been identical, just in time for the negative headlines to start around neocloud credit spreads and capex plans.

Here’s another take on the correlation question. The top panel shows the equity drawdown and the bottom panel shows the 260-week and 13-week correlation. With the exception of the dot com bust, the 13-week correlation eventually turned positive again once the scare was over. That tells us that growth scares do not move the correlation needle for long unless they turn into a recession. If today’s scare (if it’s even that) remains only scare and not a reality, I expect the relationship between equities and bonds to resume the post-2021 pattern.

Below I highlighted a few cycles where the shorter-term correlation went down or even turned negative while the structural correlation regime was positive. The LTCM growth scare and the tariff tantrum come to mind, as well the dot com bust. You can see that the circles go from “filled” (positive) to “empty” (negative).  🧵(2/2)

With the stocks/bonds correlation coming down, does that mean the 60/40 paradigm is back? I have my doubts. The chart below shows the nominal Treasury yield on the horizontal and the 260-week (5-year) correlation between the S&P 500 index and the BBG Long Treasury index on the vertical. There is a clear pattern between the level of yields and the correlation. Very low yields produce a negative correlation and higher yields produce a positive one, until the curve turns asymptotic. The size of the circles measures the 13-week correlation to give a sense of shorter correlation cycles within the larger regime. 🧵(1/2)

If I am going to be of any help with your journey in charting...

the most important advice I will give is to use horizontal boundaries to generate trade signals.

No indicators, no complicated calculations. Keep is super simple and look for horizontal boundaries with several touch points. 

Charts will start talking to you. 

Have a good night.

There is something called "style drift". When things get bumpy people start looking for tools and methods that can put them on the right track.

You practice 2 years one method, and then jump on to another and then another. You look back 5 years passed with limited progress. 

Style drift usually catch practitioners at the most emotional time in their journey. Resist the temptation of searching for the holy grail. It doesn't exist.

You can't optimize a moving average. You can't know in advance which breakout will fail. 

Stick to simple tools, look for asymmetry in risk/reward, don't let losses get out of hand. Don't override your system. Think in terms of law of large numbers.
